utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. How such a thing can happen is, for example, on this first one it's possible that the person would have recorded when the conversation started, and on the second one they may have recorded either when the conversation ended or when they typed it and sent it to their headquarters. So a 13-minute gap is not -- in this context, is not a -- I would say not significant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Would you like me to continue or do you -- okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to the intercept, itself, did you look at the substance, that is, what the intercept was referring to, in terms of analysing whether or not there was any confluence or overlap between the two or whether or not, in fact, they reflected the same conversation?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And in this conversation, can you tell us what you looked at? What gave you the impression that it was the same conversation?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people who were speaking were identified as a General Nicolai and an interpreter of General Nicolai's and then somebody -- a general from the Main Staff of the VRS, and then the contents -- who was an unidentified person in this first conversation. And the content of the conversation was summarised as that the unidentified person conveyed information that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had six armoured personnel carriers in the area. That's one point. So maybe we should go to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay, we can do that.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- corroborating --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Or maybe if you can identify if there is anything -- if there are any other points on this document, and then we can look at the next one. How ever you prefer.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. So the six armoured personnel carriers, and that they are in the areas of Zepa and Srebrenica. Then person X is asking to warn the ABiH officers to stop the assaults.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Can we go to, please, P306. Okay, I think we have them on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And as you've indicated, this document is report number 512 from the SDB, and it indicates a time of 1530 hours?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it indicates that there was a conversation recorded between the UN General Nicolai with one of General Mladic's deputies it says?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it says: "We could not hear General Nicolai -- we could not hear General Nicolai and his interpreter, Svetlana, at all." Right?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So the person speaking in this intercept is X?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And X would be the unidentified VRS general?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could we go to, please, the second page of this document. In the English only, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you -- can you tell us what -- if you can find the references that you've indicated that are present in the Croatian-sourced intercept in this document, on this page.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: X, partway down the page, says: "What I want to say to the general is that in the last couple of days, the Muslims, using six UNPROFOR armoured personnel carriers in the area of Srebrenica." And then he goes on to say: "Your commander in Srebrenica is probably aware that we found these APCs precisely in the area between Zepa and Srebrenica." "Could you please caution your forces to remove all Muslims' heavy weapons, especially the APCs?" And then it's a bit unclear. It says "or to give us precise," and that's the end of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This particular conversation reflects the six APCs, armoured personnel carriers?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it reflects the fact that they were in the areas of Zepa and Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it also reflects the fact that the VRS general asked General Nicolai to warn the ABiH officers to stop the assault actions --

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- on the other one. And on this one it's indicated: "Caution your forces to remove all Muslims' heavy weapons," it's a spelling mistake, I think, in the -- "especially the APCs"?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in your view, was that a sufficient basis to conclude that these two documents correspond essentially to the same conversation?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were you able to ascertain who the VRS general is that's mentioned in this MUP intercept, that is, the SDB intercept?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later in some of the SDB reports, they mention that they were able to ascertain that in this report number 512, it was General Tolimir who was the one who was speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. What I'd like to do is to turn, if we could, to tab number 4. That's P310. Okay, I see that we have the document in front of us now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, what I'd like to do is, first of all, indicate what it says. This is a document that is headed "Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, 2nd -- Command of the 2nd Corps," and it talks about a radio relay station, indicating the northern site. And it's dated 9 July 1995. And within this report, there is a report that's attributed to the CSB, Security Services Centre, SDB, State Security Service of Tuzla, dated also 9 July 1995, and it's report number 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: 521. Did you have an opportunity to review this intercept?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is this the intercept that you've indicated reflects the identity of the participant in the first conversation that we've just looked at?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess I would say perhaps indirectly since --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Have you had an opportunity to review this particular intercept?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the conversation within it?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were you able to compare that to a transcript of a conversation that was recorded independently and was the subject of a search, that it was retrieved during a recent search?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in that conversation, were you able to establish a connection between these two intercepts, that is, the MUP intercept from SDB and the transcript of an intercept?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. That is indicated here, and it's 65 ter 52 -- 5624A. I have it as P698.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us what about the features of this particular conversation were you able to compare?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are -- this requires a little bit of patience and flipping through the various pages, because there are, I think, four versions of this conversation. Right, or is it three? Three, three versions of it. So, I have noted, say, five points that I think are significant in the conversation that come through, and that's in addition to the date and the time and the people who were talking. May I work through this in my -- using my own initiative, since I find it a little confusing and I would like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I'd like to do, I think it might make things a little easier --

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- is I believe we have the audiotape for this particular conversation, and it might be useful to play the audiotape, and at the same time we can follow this particular intercept, so that we can see -- and this is independently, and we can see whether or not the audiotape -- or the intercept tracks the audiotape from a different source. That might be the most efficient way to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we do that, Judge Nyambe wants to have a clarification. Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: At page 54, line 25, and 53, you refer to this report number 512.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. 512 relates to the first tab here, which is the intercept, MUP origin, that indicates a time of 1530 hours on 8 July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: It's 8 July?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's right. And in this intercept that we've now been discussing, which is report number 521, there is a reference to that -- there is a reference to report number 512, and it says: "We recorded a conversation between General Nicolai and the aggressor army Officer X. General Nicolai was looking for General Mladic. The switchboard said that he was in the field. General Nicolai then asked for the officer of the aggressor army with whom he spoke in our conversation number 512." So what I propose to do or what I'd like to do is to play a recording of that conversation, or a recording of a conversation, from a different source other than the MUP so that the Trial Chamber can hear the translation of that conversation, and at the same time look at the MUP transcript to see if it tracks the conversation that's on the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: While that tape is playing, we should be looking at 521?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: 521, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I think the booths have the transcript, and it should reflect 5624A, and that's what I would like them to read as the tape plays. And at the same time I would like to have displayed on e-court -- I think we do already -- yeah, we just need to display just the MUP transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think I've got it. Ms. Stewart has provided me with an explanation, and I would ask the Court, then, to follow along in the packets, because I understand that it can't be displayed in e-court at the same time. So that would be under tab number 4. It's the very first intercept, and hopefully you'll be able to pick up, in the translation of the tape, where it meets this transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: And just for the sake of clarity, when you say "under tab 4," it is the document behind tab 4?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The document behind tab 4. It should say: "CSB/SDB, 9 July, report number 521."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Hello." "Yes." "General, sir, I wish you a good day. I'm calling you on behalf of General Nicolai. Let me hear him out and translate." "Good afternoon to you ... and General Nicolai too." "Good afternoon to you. And after yesterday's events, I would like to tell you ..." "Hello. I can't hear anything. You'll have to repeat it all." "Hello, hello." "Hello, yes." "I did not understand anything. It's very difficult to understand. Could you please repeat?" "Yes. After the events from yesterday, at least, I want to tell you that I appreciate at least the co-operation of your forces towards my soldiers who were forced to leave their observation post. Your forces enabled them to reach Bratunac safely. However, I want my soldiers to return to their base in Potocari, where they are stationed anyway and which is located in the Srebrenica enclave." "Okay ."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, we're not able to follow the whole text, only the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. It appears that -- it appears that there is an error. Just bear with me one moment and I'll see if I can straighten that out. Let's keep going. I think it's the right one.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "I have one more question for you, but I would like to hear your answer to this first." "One more time, I say hello to General Nicolai. Please accept my condolences for the death of a UN staff member in Srebrenica. And I'm going to pass his proposal to his staff currently located in the territory of Republika Srpska."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is the Chamber able to follow at this point? We've just heard the middle passage on the second page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Hello." "Yes, I'm listening." "Very well. I expect that they will be enabled to return to their base today, and that same instructions you are going to give to your subordinate commanders."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The last part was not -- what we heard was not part of the English translation of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, are you saying that it's not in the record of the proceedings or it's not on the transcript that you have in front of you? I was unclear about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We heard, like you, I suppose, the part which we see on page 2 of the English version of the transcript: "Please accept my condolences," and so on. And it stops: "Yes, I'm listening." And everything what was heard later was not part of this translation of the transcript. We couldn't follow. That's on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The translation that I've asked you to look at is a translation of the MUP version of this intercept. What you're listening to is a tape that is not the MUP version of the intercept, but a completely independent tape. So -- but you have a copy of that transcript. It's also behind the MUP one. But I wanted you to look at this MUP transcript to see if you can follow the otherwise independent conversation taken by a completely different agency to see if there's -- to see if there's an overlap or confluence among those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I see this is at the end of the pages of tab 4, at the very end, we have the B/C/S version, and before that, three pages of the English translation of that B/C/S version. And we see there, on page 2 of this English version, mentioning the condolences for the death of the UN staff member, and then it goes on, I think, as we heard it now on the audio.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: As I understand you, Mr. Vanderpuye, what we have in the folder, page 2, is the MUP transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Okay. And what we're hearing audio is an independent recording of this MUP conversation?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Okay. But just to be fair to you, there is -- a lot of the conversation here does not appear in the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct. And, in fact, what you can see in the MUP conversation or in the MUP transcript is that there's only one half of the conversation that's recorded. It's all X speaking, because it says, at the beginning -- at the beginning, you can see after that X responded, and it's only X that follows in the transcript. So what you're hearing is one side of the conversation -- what you're seeing is one side of the conversation, and you're hearing the other side of the conversation as well. And that's reflected in the transcript, although unfortunately it's not coming off as I'd hoped. It's reflected in the transcript of the tape-recording that you're hearing now. So there are parts of the tape-recording that are being translated to you that you will not see in the MUP recording -- MUP transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Okay. I understand, I hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think we're almost there, I think we're almost there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But we realise the difficulty the witness was going through during her work with the OTP. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. President, this audio-recording indicates that the transcription was selective and that they left out what didn't suit them. You could see in the first transcript, which was erroneously shown here by the Prosecutor, that General Nicolai was thanking us for releasing or letting his soldiers go, and here the general and the Prosecutor claim that he was not thanking us that we had captured them. So you can see how facts can be twisted. I would like to have this entire transcript shown, if it is available, so that we can see what this is all about. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, what is your position to that objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, I don't think it really pertains to the issues that are before the Court just now. That's number 1. Number 2 is that he does have a copy of the transcript, and he has the tape as well, and he's perfectly free to either play it or to review it and to raise any objection that he has as to either its content or any interpretation of it. Ms. Frease, I should emphasise, is not engaged in analysing the factual context or the meaning of these intercepts. She's simply engaged in comparing the two to determine whether or not they are reliable and they are authentic. And when you have two versions of a conversation that are independent of one another, then I think that's a relevant issue, in terms of what Ms. Frease is here to testify about. And clearly, there's another one that I will play to the Court where you can actually listen to the voice on the tape and ascertain for yourself, I think, relatively important information from it. But in this particular instance, all I want to do is to illustrate that there is a MUP version of this material and there is a secondary version of this material that's not related to the MUP, where the two clearly coincide and identify these two documents or these two instances as the same conversation. That's all. So whether or not it means one thing or another is completely a different story. She's not a military analyst. We're not making any representations as to the circumstances that are attendant to the intercepts, other than the fact that they overlap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now, I would appreciate if we again can continue with our examination of the witness. We were discussing the video and audio -- not the video, the audio and different transcripts. We should continue the examination of the witness. But first, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I wasn't addressing the question to the witness. I was making an objection about the way of the Prosecutor's questioning of two witnesses about one and the same event. My objection was that they were serving the Trial Chamber information that they wanted them to know and were, therefore, influencing the opinion of the Trial Chamber. As far as General Nicolai was concerned, he said that the Serbian soldiers did not save the Dutch soldiers. But at the beginning of the transcript, we saw that they did and that he was thanking. So this is serving up information to the Trial Chamber that the Prosecution would like the Trial Chamber to have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber will give weight to everything which is in front of the Trial Chamber, at the end of the day, and we have much material about this conversation and especially with the involvement of General Nicolai. We have his full testimony, with all additional exhibits. And we will examine that very carefully, you can be sure. We should continue the examination of the witness in order to save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just want to point out we're not quite at the end of the tape, which goes through to 16:41:9 in the counter, but I think we can move on from this point. What I would like to do, though, is I would like to refer the Trial Chamber, if I could, to the last -- I'd like to refer you to the last page of the MUP transcript. That should be page 3 behind tab 4. And at the same time, I'd like to refer you to the last page of the transcript of the audio material which you just heard, and that's -- for the record, it's P698. And I don't know if it's possible to display these both in e-court, but I'll ask maybe the witness if she could read those out into the record so it's very clear what the basis of her conclusions are with respect to this material. So it should be page 3 -- if we're doing it in e-court, it's page 3 of P310. There we go. And it should be page 3 of P698. I think we've got the same document on both sides. We should have, on one side, P310, and on the other side, P698. Is that what we have? Okay. No, that's not what we have. The left one, P310, should have an ERN reading "0320-5142." Well, you know, since we all have the binders in front of us, maybe we should proceed that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Ms. Frease, would you mind reading into --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Why don't we leave what we have on the screen now. Okay, we've got it. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I'd like to do is compare this attribution to X on the left to what we have on the right.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: So first you'd like me to read the attribution to X on the left, the last --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: First, let me ask did you consider --

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- what you have in front on the screen, and then tell us what it says and why you considered it important.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SDB intercept says -- the last sentence is, again, attributed to X: "I'm going to issue necessary orders immediately by telegram so the Muslims cannot listen to it and create obstacles. I hope we are going to have a positive outcome of what we have agreed here. "Regards to you, Svetlana, and to the general. Thank you for your patience and understanding." On the document on the right, the transcript of the tape, it's attributed to General Tolimir. It says: "Thank you, General. I am going to issue necessary orders immediately by telegrams so that the Muslims cannot listen to it and create obstacles. I hope we are going to have a positive outcome of what we have agreed here. Regards to you, Svetlana, and to the general. Thank you for your patience and understanding." And then that one continues because it's possible for them to hear the interpreter on that side, and she says: "Thank you. That is all for now." And his response is: "This is all for now."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you consider that important in linking these two conversations to one another as one and the same?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were other factors as well, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And could you tell us, briefly, what those are? You don't necessarily have to show us, so that we can move along in terms of time, but --

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure. There were two other points in comparing the MUP transcript to the audio transcript, and the two other points are found earlier in the conversation, where X says: "One more time, regards to General Nicolai. Please accept my condolences for the death of a UN staff member in Srebrenica. I am going to pass his proposal to his staff currently located in the Republika Srpska." And then the other one is a few lines down and talks about -- he says -- X says: "I am not informed that my commanders prevented the evacuation of the body by land. I would ask the general to send by land his team towards Bratunac, and I will immediately order that they are accepted and escorted to Zvornik." And then it goes on to talk about the helicopter flight that will take the body out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to this particular intercept, did you review also a UN report?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And that's, for the record, P682. Maybe we can have that displayed on the screen and you can tell us how that figured in your review of this material.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also consider this document to be very strong corroboration of the SDB document and the audio transcript or the audiotape that we heard, for a number of reasons: One, because of the date, it having taken place on the 12th of July; the fact that the telephone conversation indicates that it's between General Nicolai and General Tolimir, and that it's taking place at, they indicate here, 12.30. The SDB intercept records the time at 12.40. So, again, I consider that close enough in time that it's significant. And then there are five paragraphs in this document. They are notes written by Lieutenant-Colonel De Ruiter about the conversation that his general had with General Tolimir. And if you go through each of the paragraphs, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and you go through the transcript that we -- you go through the audiotape of the transcript that we just heard, you will find the same content in the audiotape of the transcript as one -- I could go through and show you where they are. Some of the conversations relate to information that is being conveyed by General Nicolai, and some of it is information that's being conveyed by General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could you just -- without necessarily directing us to where, specifically, it is in the audiotape, could you just say what those -- what those specific aspects are that you -- that you're referring to in the UN report that's reflected in the audio?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. So the first point would be the fact that the interpreter is saying that: "Your forces," the Serb forces, in other words, "enabled them, "the UN forces," to reach Bratunac safely. However, I want my soldiers to return to their base in Potocari, where they are stationed anyway, and which is in the Srebrenica enclave." So that is reflected in the first paragraph of Lieutenant-Colonel De Ruiter's note. The second point is on the next page of the transcript where General Tolimir is sending his condolences for the death of the UN staff member in Srebrenica, and that's reflected in the second paragraph of the -- of Lieutenant-Colonel De Ruiter's note. The third point is a couple of lines down, where it says -- it's the interpreter now speaking on behalf of General Nicolai, and says that: "General Nicolai --" Well, she's saying: "I expect that they will be unable to return to their base today and that the same instructions you are going to --" sorry, "and that the same instructions you are going to give to your subordinate commanders." And that's reflected in paragraph 3 of the UN note. The next point, point 4, I would say, has to do with the transportation of the body of the deceased Dutch soldier by land to Zvornik, and then by helicopter from Zvornik to Tuzla, to Zagreb. That's reflected in the fourth paragraph of the UN note. And the final point has to do with General Tolimir's comment that he was not informed by commanders that the body had been prevented -- the body was not being allowed to be evacuated by land. That's reflected in the fifth paragraph of the UN note.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to go to tab number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Before I do, let me just ask you this: As I indicated in response to a question from Her Honour Judge Nyambe, in this tab 4, P310, MUP intercept, we have an attribution of -- well, it says that the same -- the same officer of the aggressor army is the person who spoke in report number 512?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And that is -- corresponds to the communication in tab number 1, which I think you can see. Did you consider that, in terms of reaching the conclusion as to who was speaking in the conversation that's under tab number 1?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And then also under tab 6, to go to the reliability of the MUP information, the MUP had made -- the SDB had made a note where they say -- this is under tab 6, under record number 528.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. That will be, for the record, P312 -- I'm sorry, P314. It is a MUP report number 528, and you'll find that under tab 6, and it's the third-to-last page in that tab.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And could you just tell us what that says? We can avoid displaying that in e-court. What gave you that impression?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says that -- the SDB made a notation, and I quote: "It should also be pointed out that in the record number 512, a person X was, in fact, aggressor Officer General Tolimir, which we subsequently found out."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. What I'd like to do now is go to tab 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in this case, can you tell us if you had an opportunity to compare the intercepts and the materials that are under that tab?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: For the record, tab 6 contains P701. Tab 5 contains P699, P311, P680, and P700.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us how you went about reviewing these documents and what, if anything, you found among them?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went through a similar process as we've just been through, always starting with the date and the time, and then looking for information that is somewhat unique, that stands out as being very specific to a particular conversation, in addition, of course, to the participants, the people who are noted as speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in respect of this particular material, can you tell us what you found among it -- among these documents that corresponded to one another, if anything?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This conversation took place on the 9th of July, 1995. The first entry is a Croatian intercept that's recorded at 1755. The MUP intercept -- the SDB intercept notes the 9th of July, 1995, at a time of 1815, so that's 20 minutes later. The next entry are again UN notes made about the conversation on the 9th of July. This time, the time is noted as 1750, so close to the time of the first -- the first notation -- closer to the time of the first notation. And then the final entry is a transcript of the conversation that does not note a time or a date. It can't. It's an audio-recording, so it doesn't have that. But we can see that the conversation took about 15 minutes. So that also -- could also help account for the difference in time between when these took -- when the various agencies recorded that the conversation took place. In addition to that, the person -- the persons noted as speaking in the first conversation, in the Croatian summary of this conversation, is General Tolimir and General Micolai. The SDB conversation notes the same participants, though they note UN General Nicolai and say "probably Talimir." So, yeah, they spell it T-a-l-i-m-i-r. The third entry are the UN notes, which note that the conversation took place between General Nicolai and General Tolimir. And then there are three or four points in the conversation that run through these four different versions of that conversation. The first one is the fact that -- in the brief summary, the Croatian summary, that General Nicolai demanded that the VRS forces urgently withdraw some 4 kilometres to the south of their present locations. That's one point. Another point has to do with -- during the conversation, Tolimir denied that the VRS forces were around 1 kilometre from Srebrenica and claimed that the VRS forces in this area were not conducting offensive operations. And the third point in this summary is -- has to do with a UN helicopter flight that was arranged to take place the evening of the 9th of July from Tuzla-Zvornik-Split -- sorry, Tuzla-Zvornik/Tuzla-Split route for transporting the body of the UNPROFOR DutchBat soldier. So in looking at the -- I guess I would turn to the telephone conversation between General Nicolai and General Tolimir, and in the first paragraph, both the 4 kilometres and the 1 kilometres are mentioned. In the fourth paragraph down, the route of the dead soldier is mentioned from the Zvornik Stadium -- this will come up in the transcripts, but the Zvornik Stadium, and then the helicopter going en route from Tuzla to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just for the record, you're referring to P680, and that's the UN report --

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- dated 9 July 1995 at 1750 hours. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then on the transcript, there's also mention of the 4 kilometres and the 1 kilometre -- mention of the 4 kilometres a couple of different times. And then also there are additional details that come up in the actual transcripts, and a couple of those have to do with the UN soldiers being allowed to return to their base in Potocari. And then there is also a grid here that is discussed for the -- that has been crossed, and that's grid 735838. There is also reference to the fact that the UN had prevented -- managed to prevent the ABiH forces from taking their heavy weapons from the collection point, and that -- and: "We are therefore forced to defend the safe area." That comes through also in paragraph 3 of the UN report, notes from the report, that specific grid, 735838, and the fact there's an acronym here, "WCP," used in the UN report, which is the weapons collection point, which is referred to in the transcript, the lengthier transcript, the final transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you say "the lengthier transcript," you're referring to the transcript of the audiotape?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And for the record, that is P700.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And then there's also -- you know, it's a small point, but in the audio transcript, on page 3 there's this reference to the helicopter flight from Zvornik-Tuzla and from Tuzla to Split, which is the route that was first referenced in the Croatian summary of that conversation, where they say: "Tuzla-Zvornik/Tuzla-Split route." That's a general overview of the analysis among those four sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I'd like to do is I'd like to play a little bit of this recording. It's quite long, and it's only for the purposes of, one, having you, Ms. Frease, confirm that it is the tape that corresponds to this transcript. And I think it would also benefit the Trial Chamber, as this particular intercept is attributed to General Tolimir, to be able to hear the voice that's on the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So I don't think that there's any translation that's necessary for these purposes, so that you can actually hear the speakers on the audio material. It's tab 5. It's 65 ter 3466A.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And, Ms. Frease, I'd just ask you to follow along in the transcript so you can confirm that it's the right one.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I think that's all I need to play, I think, at this point. We're just about done. There are just a couple of documents I wanted to show the witness that we'd spoken about a little bit earlier, in terms of qualifying them, and then I will conclude my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That would be appreciated because of the length of the whole examination. But I think we should have our second break now, and we will resume at 10 minutes past 6.00. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Ms. Frease, we just left off with tab 5 of this group of 12 intercepts, with related documents, and I just wanted to -- I wanted to ask you if you could refer to tab 10 of this binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: For the record, tab 10 contains two documents. The first one is a Croatian intercept, and I just -- I'm looking for the P number. I don't have it written on my folder here. It's 65 ter 5554. And the second document is a MUP transcript. It's P315. The first one is P775.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to review this document?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in relation to this document, were you also able to hear audio materials relating to this intercept?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. But you did review the transcript of it?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And did the transcript conform to the -- well, the transcript of the MUP intercept conform to the Croatian intercept?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us how?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conversations are listed as taking place on the 10th of July. The Croatian version, at 2010; on the SDB MUP version, at 2015. The participants in both conversations are listed as General Janvier, Bernard Janvier, and General Zdravko Tolimir. The substance of the -- well, the summary by the -- done in the Croatian intercept says that General Janvier demands that the VRS stop attacking the UN troops south of Srebrenica and to retreat to their previous positions from the previous evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you find that reflected in the conversation?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not marked it here, but yes. The Croatian intercept goes on to say that: "General Tolimir promises he will establish contact with the commander of the Serbian unit located south of Srebrenica and order to stop the attack." So partway through the transcript, he says that he'll check with the commander in the area: "He hasn't reported to me that there's been any attack. I'll check this information and will be in touch."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, if you look over on page 3 of the MUP transcript, do you see a reference here where it says -- about the fourth entry --

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- where it says: "Yes, I do. Tell the general that, in the first place, I will establish contact with the units in order to prevent the conflict situation between UNPROFOR and the VRS. Translate."

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you can see that reflected in the Croatian intercept, do you, at about three or four lines from the bottom?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. General Janvier has information that the VRS members are attacking the UN members with two tanks, it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it says: "General Tolimir promises that he will establish contact with the commander of the Serbian unit located south of Srebrenica." Is that -- did you consider that as corroborative, at least, of these two documents?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you recall listening to any tapes in which General Tolimir actually introduced himself?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you see -- in this particular document, page 2 of the MUP transcript, it reads: "T: I am listening to you. Give General Janvier my regards." And P says: "General Janvier sends his regards, as well as says good evening, General." T says: "Good evening, General, sir. My regards. General Tolimir speaking." Do you recall listening to an audio of this particular intercept?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you recall listening to an audio, separate and apart from the MUP audio, of this particular conversation?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe the other audio starts at a different place than this -- than this transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was that the audio of material that was obtained by a search, a recent search?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did the audio conform to the transcript, as you listened to it and read the transcript, from a certain point forward?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the audio that was obtained as a result of a seizure started at a different point beyond the introduction that's attributed to General Tolimir in this conversation?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was it the case that the MUP audio contained the introduction that we see in the transcript here?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my recollection, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And with respect to all the materials in here, have you had an opportunity to go through them carefully to determine whether or not they coincide with one another?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have had an opportunity to go through all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do they, in your opinion -- do they corroborate one another so as to support the idea that they are authentic and reliable?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I wanted to show you just a couple of other documents before we get -- we're finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could just have, in e-court, please, 65 ter P859.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is unrelated to this material, but has to do with the binder of photocopied intercept material that we referred to earlier in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the record, that is Exhibit P859.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recognise that binder?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And what do you recognise it to be?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise it to be the original binder that we received the 550 pages or so of transcripts from the ABiH, Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, of intercepted conversations in July, from the 9th of July to the 31st of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And if we could just have a look at P860. I see it's invisible.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you able to see it at all on your monitor, Ms. Frease?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, that slight typewritten -- no, not really.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay, that's all right. We'll see if we can get a better photocopy to the Trial Chamber on this one. But let me ask you if you recall -- do you recall that the binder of material came with a receipt indicating that it contained 548 pages or about that number of pages?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that there was a cover page. I don't remember that it said "548 pages," but in my mind it's always been 550 pages. That's just a number that --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that. I wanted to show you another exhibit, which is 863, P863.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Have you seen this document before? Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I haven't seen it for a long time, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And this is a document that's entitled "Report of the Visual Information Branch, Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, and Fire-Arms"?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In it, it talks about specimens Q1 through Q19 received from the G2 headquarters of the 2nd Corps of Bosnia-Herzegovina Army?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And does this relate to -- what does this relate to, if you can just tell us briefly?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It relates to the 19 tapes that Jack Hunter took possession of on the 25th of April, 1998, at -- from -- that he was given at 2 Corps headquarters in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that. Just bear with me for one moment. All right. I just want to show you one last thing, and that's a map. It's P762. Okay, I think that's fine. If you could just blow it up a little bit in the area of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recognise this, by the way, Ms. Frease?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Does it represent locations that are indicated in the intercepts that you reviewed in preparation for either this testimony or the Popovic case?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell me or tell the Trial Chamber what those locations are?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stublic, Zepa. Those are the only two that I remember from the intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That concludes my direct examination, finally, and I appreciate the Trial Chamber's indulgence. Thank you, Ms. Frease.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The examination-in-chief took a long time, much longer than expected. We will come back to your tendering of exhibits, not to use more court time with these procedural matters. So, Mr. Tolimir, it's now up to you to start your cross-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to greet the witness. Since we speak the same [as interpreted] language, we'll pause between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all background noise please seized and could Mr. Tolimir be asked to turn his microphone towards him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please clarify for the Chamber, what is your understanding of authenticity and reliability of certain material, since you mostly addressed the issue of authenticity and reliability, both you and the Prosecutor, during examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand the word "authenticity" to talk about the genuineness of material, whether it is what it purports to be, whether it comes from the sources that it purports to come from. And the term "reliability" I would use to describe the consistency within that material, the content of the material. That would also, in this case, go to the procedures that were followed in order to create it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please tell us whether the document you saw for the first time, the one you referred to yesterday, dated sometime in 2008, is also authentic. It was line 1 through to 7, page 67. Is it, in your opinion, authentic, although you saw it only then? And based on that document you saw for the first time, you mentioned the authenticity of another document shown to you by the Prosecutor. For reference, it is page 67, lines 1 through 7.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to know the specific document to which you're referring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please give us the document number so that we can have it on the screen and the witness knows what she's asked.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The document was shown yesterday at page 67, lines 1 through 7, when the witness addressed the issue of authenticity. Maybe the document was number 67, although I'm not certain. I wasn't able to write it down. I didn't have time to note down the exact reference. To remind the witness, it seems to have been a document from the Krstic and Popovic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think the witness has seen so many documents in the course of the examination, it is necessary to identify it. Otherwise, we are all lost and don't know what you're talking about. Please, with the assistance of your team, it should be possible to find out the correct number of that document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I think I gave the right reference, line 1 to 7, page 67. And my legal consultant believes it is P785.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We will try to have it on the screen. We were asking not for the reference of yesterday, but for the document number. P785.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The document P785 is a map.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I did manage to note down that it was a map. But could we please have page 67, lines 1 to 7, shown to the witness? I believe we all recall the situation when she was asked whether it was authentic, and the witness said that she saw it for the first time in the Krstic and Popovic case in 2008, I believe. You even asked whether it could be authentic for the simple reason that you saw it in 2008, if you recall that. I don't have the transcript before me and I have to follow my notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we are all in the same position. Even if we see the transcript of yesterday, I'm not sure if we find the correct document. We have to show the document to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could we please have page 67, lines 1 to 7, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think I have a reference and that might facilitate matters, I think. It's page 5.028 in the transcript, I believe, and maybe I can read it into the record so that Mr. Tolimir can verify that that's the right one, and maybe we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That would be helpful. Thank you very much, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. It reads as follows: "And in connection with what case did you prepare this authentication binder of material?" "The first time was for the Krstic case." "And did you prepare a second one?" "Yes." "When was that and for what purposes -- when was that and for what case?" "In the Popovic case." This is the only reference to first time that's in the vicinity of the transcript that Mr. Tolimir is referring to, and it's page 68 of yesterday's transcript, but there's no reference to a document at page 67 that the witness has said was the first time that she's seen it. So perhaps that -- I don't know if that actually -- perhaps that clarifies the situation, but it certainly doesn't seem to indicate that page 67 is the right one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And I think now we see the problem. We don't have the -- and especially the Registry doesn't have the page number 67, because it is now added to the previous transcripts and it's now about 4.900 and something, so that the Registry is not in the position to identify this portion of the transcript of yesterday by the page numbers of yesterday's transcript alone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. But you can see here what my problem is. From the beginning, three years that I've been here, I did not get a transcript from a status conference, never mind from the proceedings. Mr. Vanderpuye now has read the transcript, which is in English, which I'm unable to use, and I'm handicapped there. And you remember the witness saying this yesterday. Perhaps if Mr. Vanderpuye would be kind enough, he could read to us what you said, what the Presiding Judge asked the witness. My question was: Is it an authenticity matter, when you see the document for the first time, and you confirm whether it is the document that the Prosecutor is putting his questions on? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm just looking at the transcript of yesterday and trying to find the portion where I am putting questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This is from that part that Vanderpuye has read out. He read out the reference that I was talking about. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If you are referring to that part of the transcript of yesterday which Mr. Vanderpuye was reading, then you should put the question to the witness again. Perhaps that was helpful to understand the background of your question. I don't find it at the moment, like you don't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Since I don't have the transcript, I'm going to rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Would any document be authentic that is drafted today, but discusses events that took place at the time of the events in Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the context of what we've been discussing, the documents that I've been referring to relate -- relate to or were created, in large part, at the time of those events. In general, I guess I would probably say no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, are you able to clarify what the difference is, in your mind, between the term "authenticity" and the term "reliability"? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think I tried to do that above. To me, "authenticity" goes to the genuineness of the document, to the agency or individual that created it, where the reliability of the document refers more to -- one way to think about it is the internal content, the internal procedures that were followed in the creation of that document. That's the way that I think about those two issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall when Mr. Vanderpuye asked you yesterday whether you had taken part in the interception of the conversations, and you said, Yes? This was on page 56 of the transcript. Probably we would need to add a number to it. I mean, it was line 8, minute 21. This is what I'm able to note down. He also asked you on page 57, line 13, whether you had taken part in the creation of the database, and you answered: "Yes, I was engaged in the entire process." Later, he asked whether you testified here about the authenticity of the creation of the database, and you said: "Yes." So what you authorised, you state that it is authentic. I'm not denying that. But based on what you compiled or authored, can it be authentic in relation to something that happened 15 years ago, particularly when we see that there are differences in the content? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't recall saying that I had taken place in the interception of conversations. If that is anywhere in the transcript, it should not be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the transcript, it said that you compiled databases, you created databases. Perhaps the translation was wrong. Tomorrow, we are going to provide the transcript lines and these pages the way that they are marked here from the markings of the Registry, and then you will be able to see that. And then when my legal advisor sees the original, the transcript, since I don't have it, I have no intention of asking you anything that you didn't say. If you didn't say something, I apologise immediately, but we will check this tomorrow. All I want you to do now is to tell us whether there is a major difference between the way a lawyer, an artist, or an architect understands the term "authenticity," or a scientist. The same would apply for the term "reliability." Would a philosopher or an analyst or a lawyer understand this term differently?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to go back to one of your previous questions or statements that said that I had testified also yesterday about the authenticity of the creation of the database. Again, I do not believe that I was asked that question and that I would have responded to it positively, only that I was involved in creating a database. But that is a question that's very separate from the authenticity of the material that was entered into the database. When we analysed the material, when we entered the material into the database, we were extremely careful not to summarise the information and not to put our own interpretation on the material that we entered. I was extremely strict on this point with myself and with other team members. We used the words --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We used the words that came through in the material that we were using. We did not alter the words that came to us, and that was very important. It was a very important internal principle, because as information comes in on an investigation, words can take on new meanings. And if, internally, we were putting our own meaning on words, it could alter the way that those conversations could later be interpreted by another member of the investigation that had received other information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please look at the transcript from yesterday, page 5017, lines 13 to 14. And if you can tell us what is stated there, because I don't know English and I wrote down what I said back to you. You said: "I took part in that whole process. I was very engaged." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm quite confident that the witness doesn't have a copy of the transcript in front of her. I have found the indicated page and reference by Mr. Tolimir, which I can read into the record, and perhaps Mr. Gajic can read it into the record so the witness is clear -- oh, Ms. Stewart advises me that she can show it on Sanction so the witness can see it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which lines?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think it was 13 and 14, page 5017.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the question was: "And were you involved in any way in assembling or putting all of these intercepts together in 2006 for the Prosecution?" Is that the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That is how it was translated back to me, and this is what I literally wrote, because I'm writing down, like a stenographer, exactly what is being interpreted back to me. So I cannot be blamed for what I heard yesterday. What I hear is what I take at face value. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, just to clarify one matter, nobody is blaming you. Especially the examination of this witness, with so many different documents, it's very complicated for all of us, including you. No problem at all. Nobody is blaming you. And I think now the witness has heard this part and could see it, and I think we should wait for the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My answer is, yes, that I was involved in assembling and cross-referencing and putting together the intercepts for the Popovic trial. I was not responsible for the final selection of the intercepts, but I was certainly very involved in compiling the various versions of the intercepts as we've been discussing; the note-books, the print-outs, the electronic versions, all of that material, and the transcript -- and the audio.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Earlier, towards the end of the examination-in-chief, we saw a document that accompanied an audio-recording. And we saw that the document, the transcript, follows the audio up to a certain point in time, and then you can hear the audio segment, but this is not recorded in the transcript. Can you please tell me whether that transcript is both authentic and reliable? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you clarify which audio-recording and which transcript you're referring to, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that that is document P306, which was recorded at 1517 hours, and I'm thinking of the document P512, which was recorded at 1530 hours. Does this speak to the authenticity and reliability of these documents, in line with the criteria of a court? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, this --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We can see both documents here that were recorded at 1530 hours. We need P306, which was recorded at 1517 hours, and the document by the SDB, 512, which was recorded on the 8th of July at 1530. And you said that this was not a significant difference. I'm asking you whether they speak to the reliability and authenticity of each one. And this is in tab 1 of your binder.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. In my view, this goes to -- more to the genuineness and to the -- you could say genuineness or authenticity of the sources of both of these conversations, one that was picked up by the Croatians, and the other that was picked up by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina -- or, sorry, by the MUP, by the SDB.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm sorry, I just want to intervene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want to intervene for a moment. Mr. Tolimir is referring to P306, which is, in fact, the MUP intercept that's indicated at 1530. The Croatian report is at 1517. And for the record, that's P786, just so that we can get that in e-court if he needs it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I was told the first number we received was the wrong one. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While looking at the document on the right-hand side, the Prosecutor also played the audio-recording, in which we could follow a part of the conversation. Later, Judge Nyambe asked, Why wasn't the entire footage reflected in the transcript. So my question is: Does this satisfy the criteria of reliability, because something could have been said there that was quite important to the accused or for one of the parties in these proceedings? There is a difference of 20 minutes here. In those 20 minutes, we're going to find, in these note-books, scores of other conversations that last for a minute or two minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe your second reference to the audio refers to tab 4. Is that possible? So we've moved on from tab 1 to tab 4; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. It's possible, because you know this better because you looked at those documents. But I just remember what happened just now. We saw -- and Judge Nyambe asked you whether this was a small time difference here. That is why I'm asking you why a part of the text is missing, whereas it can be heard in the audio-recording. So what I'm asking you is: Would this indicate that -- would the authenticity principle apply to this?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir is asked to repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think we're talking about two different things. The first one we were talking about, tab 1, where one of the -- where the Croatian intercept records a time of 1517 and where the BiH MUP, SDB, police intercept, records the conversation at 1530. I mentioned that's a difference of 13 minutes, and to me that's not a significant difference, because it's possible that the MUP -- that the police could have recorded the time when the conversation ended and not when the conversation started. And then there's also just a factor of people's watches or the clocks that they're looking on the wall. I'm sure that if we all compare the times that we have on our watches now, they're going to be different. So that's one issue. The second issue, I think, does relate to tab 4, where we were -- the Prosecutor asked us to look at the MUP transcript while playing a longer version of that same transcript. And what one should note in the MUP transcript is that because of their location, as we've discussed before, they were only able to hear one side of the conversation. So I think that was the one where I went through five points, and really only points 2 and 5 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That is a different question. We will come to that. Thank you. This is a different question. We are going to discuss the contents -- I just want to finish.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just want to finish what I was saying, if I may, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If you, in your analysis of short conversations that we had here, miss out one word only, or part of a sentence, or an entire sentence, because we could see that a few sentences were missing from the text that we were looking at today, could that change the content of the entire conversation or the flow of the entire conversation? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And also re-telling it, as we could see today on the left-hand side, a kind of summary or re-telling, the process of re-telling also possibly can change the whole course of a conversation, as you can see. Perhaps you can see here some examples. You have the place where it says "General Nikolin" instead of "General Nicolai," so one letter can change the sense, and we are re-telling, summarising, this conversation. So could you please tell us whether this summary process -- the process of summarising can also change the course of a conversation? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in this exercise, what we were doing was talking about the authentication of the intercepts, as a whole, and the process that I and my colleagues undertook to ensure that the intercepts were genuine or authentic. Now, in the Croatian intercepts, in the ones that we mostly have here, you do find summaries, and my sense of why that is the case is that these were not of a high priority for the agency that was intercepting them, so they wrote a summary. There isn't -- I haven't seen anything in the summaries --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Just -- just answer my question. Thank you, thank you. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen anything in the summaries that contradict the longer transcripts that we have that were completed by other agencies or other bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. It has shown in front of this Tribunal that General Gvero and I spoke with General Nicolai. How could you tell here who was speaking with General Nicolai, myself or Gvero? The Trial Chamber heard both transcripts. And does this summarising change the sense? And I'm not asking you anything else. I know how things came about or how they were created, but this is all I'm asking you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And this is, indeed, the last question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I am sorry for exceeding the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went through a process to show that it was you speaking in this conversation, through looking at other conversations that were recorded by the SDB in Tuzla referencing these various numbers. And I guess at that point, one does get into the reliability and the process that was used and that was followed by the particular agencies, which is why I consider the material to be both authentic and reliable. And in this particular example, we could go through, again, if necessary, the process that was used to determine that the general speaking to General Nicolai was you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have to stop here for today. First of all, I would like to express my and the Chamber's and the participants' apologies to the interpreters, to the whole staff of the Tribunal, for the extended sitting. We are running out of time. But talking about time: The clock in the courtroom shows some seconds after 10 minutes past 7.00, the LiveNote shows 1908 hours, and my private clock shows me seven minutes past 7.00. This is only a remark to the exact time we are following. We are running out of time. We have to continue the day after tomorrow, because tomorrow is a UN holiday. We are not working tomorrow. On Friday, in the afternoon, 2.15, in Courtroom III. We have to adjourn, and please be reminded that it is not permitted to have contact with either party about the content of your examination during the break. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 10th day of September, 2010, at 2.15 p.m. 24 25
